module.title: Propositional Logic
module.description: Module 1 introduces the foundations of propositional logic. v3 reorganizes the v2 pilot to remove the rigid hook → why-it-matters → storytelling pattern; each lesson now follows a flow shaped to its own concept. Storytelling appears INLINE only at moments where a real student would naturally ask. Every visual carries renderable data.
source_files: CPCS 222 - Lab 02 Applications of propositional logic.pdf

lessons.title: What Is a Proposition?
lessons.welcome: Logic, mathematical proofs, and even university registration rules all rest on a single atom: a sentence that is definitely true or false. This lesson nails down exactly which sentences qualify.
objectives: Define a proposition and identify its truth value.
Distinguish propositions from questions, commands, exclamations, and open sentences.
Assign propositional variables (p, q, r) to atomic propositions.
Recognize the standard 'not-a-proposition' traps used on labs and exams.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Professor, why is `x > 5` not a proposition? It looks mathematical.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Because x is free. Until you pick a value or quantify x, the sentence has no fixed truth value. Plug in x = 7 and you get the true proposition '7 > 5'; plug in x = 2 and you get the false proposition '2 > 5'. The original is just a TEMPLATE.

flow.title: Proposition
flow.content: A **proposition** is a declarative sentence that is either **true (T)** or **false (F)**, but never both.

Two checks are needed for a sentence to be a proposition:

1. It must be **declarative** (a statement, not a question or a command).
2. It must have a **definite truth value** right now — no free variables, no missing context.

Both checks must pass. Failing either one disqualifies the sentence.

flow.title: Quick gallery
rows: Jeddah is on the Red Sea.

flow.trigger: After the gallery a student typically asks the open-sentence question.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: So `x + 2 = 7` is not a proposition because of x?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Right. Free variables disqualify a sentence. Plug in x = 5 and it becomes the proposition '5 + 2 = 7' (true). Plug in x = 1 and it becomes '1 + 2 = 7' (false). The original is a template, not a proposition.

flow.title: Don't confuse FALSE with NOT-A-PROPOSITION
flow.content: A wrong claim like 'KAU is in Riyadh' is **still a proposition** — its truth value is just F. The disqualifier is having no truth value at all, not having the wrong one.

flow.title: Around campus and Absher
items: **Proposition (T):** 'CPCS 222 is offered at King Abdulaziz University.'
**Proposition (F):** 'Tabuk is the capital of Saudi Arabia.'
**Not a proposition:** 'Open Absher and renew your iqama.' — a command.
**Not a proposition:** 'Did you pay your STC bill?' — a question.
**Not a proposition:** 'x is enrolled in CPCS 222.' — open sentence; once you fix x = 'Sara' it becomes a proposition.

flow.title: Naming atomic propositions
flow.content: Once a sentence passes both checks, we treat it as an **atomic proposition** and name it with a letter — usually p, q, r, s. Example: let `p` = 'It is raining in Jeddah' and `q` = 'I am at home'. We can now talk about `p ∧ q` ('it is raining in Jeddah AND I am at home') without rewriting the English each time. Pick a fresh letter for each fresh sentence; never reuse `p` for two different statements in the same problem.

flow.title: The two-question test
Exam-style passage
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q1 — 'identify five sentences that are not a proposition'.
flow.problem:
Read the passage and list the **non-propositions**:

_'Sara reached KAU before her CPCS 222 lecture. The library opens at 7:30 AM. Please silence your phone. 12 is divisible by 4. She wrote `x + 5 = 11` in her notebook. Wow, the lecture hall is full today!'_
flow.thinking_process: Walk through each sentence and apply the two-property test.
step_by_step_solution: 'Please silence your phone.' — **command** → not a proposition.
'`x + 5 = 11`' — **open sentence** with free x → not a proposition.
'Wow, the lecture hall is full today!' — **exclamation** → not a proposition.
flow.final_answer: Three non-propositions: the command, the open sentence, and the exclamation.
flow.common_mistake: Marking the open sentence as a proposition because it 'looks mathematical'.

flow.title: Lab 01 starter
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q1 — proposition classification.
flow.problem: Decide if each is a proposition; if so, give the truth value: (a) 'Cairo is the capital of Egypt.' (b) '5 + 7 = 10.' (c) 'x + 2 = 11.' (d) 'Answer this question.'
flow.thinking_process: Apply the two-property test once per item.
step_by_step_solution: (c) Free variable x → not a proposition.
flow.common_mistake: Calling (c) a proposition because it has an equals sign.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Thinking a **false** sentence cannot be a proposition. False propositions are still propositions.
Treating equations with free variables as propositions. They are open sentences until variables are bound or assigned.
Calling self-referential paradoxes ('this sentence is false') a proposition — it cannot consistently be either T or F.

flow.title: Two-Question Test
flow.content: Declarative? Definite truth value? Both YES → proposition. Anything else: not a proposition.

sections.heading: The two-property test
sections.explanation: A sentence is a proposition iff it is declarative AND has a definite truth value. Both checks must pass.

sections.heading: Atomic propositions and naming
sections.explanation: Each simple proposition is atomic; we name atoms with letters p, q, r, s so we can manipulate them symbolically.

sections.heading: Exam-style passages
sections.explanation: Mid-term-style passages mix declarative facts with commands, questions, exclamations, and free-variable equations. The skill is fast classification.

worked_examples.problem: Read the passage and list the non-propositions: 'Sara reached KAU before her CPCS 222 lecture. The library opens at 7:30 AM. Please silence your phone. 12 is divisible by 4. She wrote x + 5 = 11. Wow, the lecture hall is full today!'
step_by_step_solution: 'Wow, the lecture hall is full today!' — exclamation.
worked_examples.final_answer: Three non-propositions: command, open sentence, exclamation.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each rejected sentence fails one of the two property checks.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Marking the open sentence as a proposition because it looks mathematical.

quick_checks.question: Which IS a proposition?
quick_checks.explanation: Declarative with a definite truth value.

quick_checks.question: A false sentence cannot be a proposition.
quick_checks.explanation: A proposition only needs a definite truth value; being false is allowed.

quick_checks.question: Why is 'y > 5' not a proposition?
quick_checks.answer: Because y is free; without a value the sentence has no definite truth value.
quick_checks.explanation: Open sentences become propositions only when their variables are bound or assigned.

key_takeaways: A proposition is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value (T or F).
Questions, commands, exclamations, and open sentences are NOT propositions.
Atomic propositions get fresh letters (p, q, r) so we can manipulate them symbolically.
Mid-term passages test fast classification over mixed sentences.
summary.next: Now we combine atomic propositions using **logical connectives** — the small symbols that act like the verbs of formal logic.

lessons.title: Logical Connectives — The Verbs of Logic
lessons.welcome: Atomic propositions are useful only once we **combine** them. Four small symbols (¬, ∧, ∨, ⊕) act like the verbs of formal logic. Each has a fixed truth table, and once you know all four you can evaluate any compound proposition by hand.
objectives: Compute the truth value of compound propositions involving ¬, ∧, ∨, ⊕.
Translate English connectives ('and', 'but', 'or', 'either…or but not both') into the right symbol.
Distinguish inclusive ∨ from exclusive ⊕ in everyday English.
Recognize the lab/exam-style translation patterns (Lab 01 Q3, Q4).

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Why do we need separate symbols ∨ and ⊕? English just says 'or'.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Because English 'or' is ambiguous. 'You may pay with mada OR Apple Pay' allows both. 'Soup OR salad with the entrée' rules out both. Logic uses ∨ for the inclusive case and ⊕ for the exclusive case so every formula has one definite meaning.

flow.content:
Imagine the KAU registration rule:

> _'You may register for CPCS 222 if you passed CPCS 203 **and** your GPA is at least 2.0.'_

This is a compound condition — two atomic conditions (passed prerequisite, GPA threshold) joined by **AND**. Logic captures this with a single symbol, **∧**, that has an unambiguous truth table. We have four such symbols this lesson.

flow.title: Negation (¬)
flow.content: **¬p** (read 'not p') flips p's truth value. If p is T, ¬p is F. If p is F, ¬p is T.

flow.title: Conjunction (∧)
flow.content: **p ∧ q** ('p AND q') is true exactly when **both** p and q are true. English 'but' is logically the same as 'and' — only the tone differs.

flow.title: Conjunction (p ∧ q)
flow.notes: True only when BOTH operands are true.

flow.title: Translating 'but'
flow.content: _'It is below freezing **but** not snowing'_ → `p ∧ ¬q`. The 'but' contributes only stylistic contrast.

flow.title: Disjunction (∨) — INCLUSIVE 'or'
flow.content: **p ∨ q** ('p OR q') is true when **at least one** of p, q is true (including the case where both are true). This is the inclusive 'or' of mathematics.

flow.title: Disjunction (p ∨ q) — INCLUSIVE 'or'
flow.notes: False only when both are false.

flow.title: Exclusive or (⊕)
flow.content: **p ⊕ q** is true when **exactly one** of p, q is true (but not both). Use this for the everyday 'either…or…but not both' phrasing.

flow.title: Exclusive or (p ⊕ q)
flow.notes: True when EXACTLY one operand is true.

flow.trigger: Right after introducing both ∨ and ⊕ — the natural moment for the question.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: How do I tell when English 'or' is inclusive vs exclusive?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Ask: would the speaker accept BOTH happening? 'You may pay with mada OR Apple Pay' — the cashier doesn't reject you for using both methods, so it is inclusive ∨. 'Soup OR salad comes with the entrée' — picking both is excluded, so it is exclusive ⊕. When in doubt, default to ∨; logic textbooks treat ∨ as the standard.

flow.title: ∨ vs ⊕ — only one row differs
flow.notes: Both connectives agree on three rows. They disagree only on (T, T): ∨ says T, ⊕ says F.

flow.title: Saudi-flavoured ∨ vs ⊕
items: **Inclusive (∨):** 'You may pay your STC bill via mada OR Apple Pay.' — both methods are accepted.
**Exclusive (⊕):** 'Either renew your driver's license at Absher OR at the Muroor office (not both — they share a record).'
**Inclusive (∨):** 'Students who took CPCS 203 OR Math 110 may register.' — both is allowed.
**Exclusive (⊕):** 'Either you arrive on time OR you miss the exam — not both.'

flow.title: Operator precedence shortcut
flow.content: When parentheses are missing, **¬** binds tightest. So `¬p ∨ q` parses as `(¬p) ∨ q`, NOT `¬(p ∨ q)`. Use parentheses if you intend the second meaning.

flow.title: Evaluating a compound proposition
items: 1. Identify the atomic variables and their truth values.
2. Compute innermost subexpressions first (negations, parenthesized parts).
3. Move outward connective by connective using each truth table.
4. The final value is the truth of the whole expression.

flow.title: Translating English to symbols
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q3 — translation with p = 'below freezing', q = 'snowing'.
flow.problem:
Let `p` = 'It is below freezing' and `q` = 'It is snowing'. Translate:
(a) 'It is below freezing **and** snowing.'
(b) 'It is below freezing **but not** snowing.'
(c) 'It is **not** below freezing **and** it is **not** snowing.'
(d) 'Either it is snowing **or** below freezing (or both).'
flow.thinking_process: Map each English connector to a symbol; apply ¬ to whichever piece is being negated.
flow.common_mistake: Negating BOTH p and q in (b) instead of only q.

flow.title: Symbolic to English
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q4 — symbolic-to-English translation.
flow.problem: Let `p` = 'Sharks have been spotted near the shore' and `q` = 'Swimming at the New Jersey shore is allowed'. Translate **¬p ∨ q** to English.
flow.thinking_process: Translate the negation, then the disjunction, paying attention to inclusive 'or'.
step_by_step_solution: ¬p = 'Sharks have not been spotted near the shore.'
¬p ∨ q = 'Either no sharks have been spotted, OR swimming is allowed (or both).'
flow.final_answer: 'Either no sharks have been spotted, or swimming is allowed (or both).'
flow.common_mistake: Reading ∨ as exclusive when translating back to English.

flow.title: Computing a compound truth value
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 02 Q5–Q7 — truth-value verification.
flow.problem: Compute `(p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q)` when p = T, q = T.
flow.thinking_process: Evaluate inside-out using each connective's truth table.
step_by_step_solution: p ∧ q = T ∧ T = T, so ¬(p ∧ q) = **F**.
flow.common_mistake: Computing the outer ∧ before the inner pieces.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Translating 'but' as anything other than ∧.
Reading every English 'or' as exclusive — the default in logic is inclusive (∨).
Forgetting that ¬ binds tighter than ∧, ∨ — `¬p ∨ q` is `(¬p) ∨ q`, not `¬(p ∨ q)`.

flow.title: Four connectives, four behaviours
items: **¬** flips the bit.
**∧** is true only when **both** are true.
**∨** is true when **at least one** is true (inclusive).
**⊕** is true when **exactly one** is true (exclusive).

sections.heading: The four connectives
sections.explanation: ¬, ∧, ∨, ⊕ each have a fixed, unambiguous truth table. ¬ takes one input; the other three take two.

sections.heading: Inclusive vs exclusive 'or'
sections.explanation: English 'or' is ambiguous; ∨ is inclusive and ⊕ is exclusive. Default to ∨ unless the context forbids both being true simultaneously.

sections.heading: Translation patterns
sections.explanation: 'And' and 'but' both → ∧. Most 'or' phrases → ∨. 'Either…or…but not both' → ⊕. Negations attach only to the piece being negated.

worked_examples.problem: Let p = 'below freezing', q = 'snowing'. Translate (a) p AND q, (b) p but not q, (c) neither.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each English connector maps cleanly to one symbol.

quick_checks.question: If p is false and q is true, what is p ∧ q?
quick_checks.explanation: Conjunction is true only when both operands are true.

quick_checks.question: Which connective best matches 'either left or right (but not both)'?
quick_checks.explanation: 'Either…or…but not both' is the textbook phrasing of exclusive or.

quick_checks.question: p ∨ q is true when both p and q are true.
quick_checks.explanation: Inclusive ∨ is true when at least one operand is true, including the both-true case.

key_takeaways: Conjunction (∧) is true only when both operands are true.
Disjunction (∨) is **inclusive** — true when at least one is true.
Exclusive or (⊕) is true when **exactly one** is true.
Evaluate compound propositions inside-out, table by table.
summary.next: Next: full **truth tables** and the trickiest connective — the conditional (→) and its cousin the biconditional (↔).

lessons.title: Truth Tables and Conditional Statements
lessons.welcome: This lesson combines two skills: building a complete **truth table** for any compound proposition, and reading the most important connective of all — the **conditional** (p → q). Get the conditional right and proofs, theorems, and registration rules all become precise.
objectives: Construct a complete truth table for a compound proposition with up to three atoms.
Define the implication p → q and explain why it is true when the hypothesis is false.
Translate the English phrasings of 'if p then q' into → form.
Form the converse, contrapositive, and inverse — and know which is logically equivalent to the original.
Define the biconditional p ↔ q and apply the standard precedence rules.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Why is `F → T` considered true? It feels arbitrary.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Think of an implication as a promise: 'If p happens, q will happen.' If p never happens, the promise is never tested. We cannot say it was broken, so by convention we count it as kept — that is, true. The only row that can break the promise is `T → F`: the trigger fired but the obligation failed.

flow.title: Building a truth table — the procedure
items: 1. Count atoms n; you will need 2ⁿ rows.
2. Write a column per atom; fill all 2ⁿ truth-value combinations.
3. Add a column for each subexpression as it grows in complexity.
4. Compute each new column from the columns to its left.
5. Verify the final column row by row.

flow.title: Row counts you'll meet most often
items: 1 atom → **2** rows
2 atoms → **4** rows
3 atoms → **8** rows
4 atoms → **16** rows
5 atoms → **32** rows

flow.title: Implication (p → q)
flow.content: **p → q** ('if p, then q') is **FALSE only when p is T and q is F**. In every other row it is T. Think of p → q as a promise: only a kept promise that fails counts as broken.

flow.title: Implication (p → q)
flow.notes: False only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false.

flow.trigger: Immediately after the implication truth table — the F→T row is the standard sticking point.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Professor, why is `F → T` considered true?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Promise framing. 'If p, then q' is a contract that can be broken in only one way: p triggers but q fails. If p never triggers, the contract is never tested — we declare it kept. That keeps the algebra clean: an unbroken promise is true.

flow.title: Implications around campus and Absher
items: _'If you submit your CPCS 222 assignment, then you receive a grade.'_ — broken only by submission + no grade.
_'If you have a valid Iqama, then you can renew your driver's license on Absher.'_ — broken only by valid Iqama + cannot renew.
_'If you scored 100 % on the final, then you get an A.'_ — broken only by 100 % + not-A.

flow.title: Many English phrases — same →
items: _'if p, then q'_
_'p implies q'_
_'p **only if** q'_
_'q if p'_
_'q whenever p'_
_'q follows from p'_
_'p is **sufficient** for q'_
_'q is **necessary** for p'_

flow.title: 'Only if' is one of the most-flipped phrases on exams
flow.content: **'p only if q'** translates to **p → q** (q is necessary for p), NOT q → p. The side that comes after 'only if' is the conclusion.

flow.trigger: Right after the 'only if' warning — students reliably ask this.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Why does 'only if' reverse the direction I expect?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Because 'only if' marks the **necessary** side. 'You can enter the exam **only if** you have your student ID' means having the ID is required; entering implies you brought the ID. So `enter → have_ID`. Read 'only if' as 'requires'.

flow.title: Converse, contrapositive, inverse
items: **Converse:** q → p
**Contrapositive:** ¬q → ¬p — **logically equivalent** to p → q
**Inverse:** ¬p → ¬q — equivalent to the converse, NOT to the original

flow.title: How the four forms relate
flow.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  O["p → q (original)"] -- equivalent --> CP["¬q → ¬p (contrapositive)"]
  CV["q → p (converse)"] -- equivalent --> IN["¬p → ¬q (inverse)"]
  O -. NOT equivalent .- CV
  O -. NOT equivalent .- IN

flow.title: Biconditional (p ↔ q)
flow.content: **p ↔ q** ('p if and only if q', often shortened to **iff**) is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value. Equivalently `p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)`.

flow.title: Biconditional (p ↔ q)
flow.notes: True exactly when p and q have the same truth value.

flow.title: Operator precedence (high → low)
items: 1. **¬** (tightest)
5. **↔** (loosest)

flow.title: Useful equivalences
items: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)

flow.title: Truth table for `(p ∨ ¬q) → q`
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q6 — truth-table construction.
flow.problem: Construct a complete truth table for **`(p ∨ ¬q) → q`** with intermediate columns for `¬q` and `p ∨ ¬q`.
flow.thinking_process: Two atoms ⇒ 4 rows. Build each column left-to-right.
step_by_step_solution: Row (T, T): ¬q = F, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → T = **T**.
Row (T, F): ¬q = T, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → F = **F**.
Row (F, T): ¬q = F, p ∨ ¬q = F, F → T = **T**.
Row (F, F): ¬q = T, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → F = **F**.
flow.final_answer: Final column: T, F, T, F.
flow.common_mistake: Skipping the intermediate ¬q column — easy to drop a sign.

flow.title: Translating 'only if'
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q4 — translate 'access only if user is authenticated and data is encrypted'.
flow.problem: Translate to logic: 'You can access the system **only if** you are an administrator OR you are not a freshman.' Use `a` = access, `d` = administrator, `f` = freshman.
flow.thinking_process: 'p only if q' → p → q. Identify hypothesis (a) and conclusion (d ∨ ¬f).
flow.common_mistake: Reversing into (d ∨ ¬f) → a. Read 'only if' as 'requires'.

flow.title: CCI in English
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q3 / Assignment 1 Q3 — converse, inverse, contrapositive in English.
flow.problem: State the **converse, contrapositive, and inverse** of: 'If you submit the CPCS 222 assignment, then you receive a grade.'
flow.thinking_process: Let p = submit, q = receive grade. Apply the three transformations.
step_by_step_solution: **Converse** (q → p): 'If you receive a grade, then you submitted the assignment.'
**Contrapositive** (¬q → ¬p): 'If you do not receive a grade, then you did not submit the assignment.'
**Inverse** (¬p → ¬q): 'If you do not submit the assignment, then you do not receive a grade.'
flow.final_answer: Three transformed sentences as listed; only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.
flow.common_mistake: Treating the converse as if it followed from the original — a grade might be received another way (late credit).

flow.title: Tautology by rules
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Assignment 1 Q4 — show [p ∧ (p → q)] → q is a tautology.
flow.problem: Show that **`[p ∧ (p → q)] → q`** is a tautology using rules (no truth table).
flow.thinking_process: Eliminate → using `p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q`; simplify with distributive, negation, and identity laws.
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting to apply De Morgan to ¬(p ∧ q).

flow.title: Top mistakes on exams
items: Reversing 'only if' into the wrong direction.
Treating the converse as equivalent to the original (only the contrapositive is).
Forgetting that F → anything = T (both rows with hypothesis F are true).
Writing ¬(p → q) ≡ p → ¬q. The correct form is `p ∧ ¬q`.

flow.title: Three rules to memorize
items: **Promise rule:** an implication is broken only on T → F.
**CCI map:** **C**ontrapositive is **C**ompletely equivalent. Converse and Inverse are not.
**Iff = both arrows:** p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p).

sections.heading: Building a truth table
sections.explanation: n atomic variables → 2ⁿ rows. Add intermediate columns for each subexpression and compute left-to-right.

sections.heading: The implication (→)
sections.explanation: p → q is false ONLY on (T, F); otherwise true. Frame it as a promise that can only be broken by the trigger firing while the obligation fails.

sections.heading: Converse, contrapositive, inverse
sections.explanation: From p → q we form three related conditionals. Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.

sections.heading: Biconditional and precedence
sections.explanation: p ↔ q is true when p and q match. Precedence: ¬ > ∧ > ∨ > → > ↔.

worked_examples.problem: Construct a truth table for (p ∨ ¬q) → q.
step_by_step_solution: Row (T,T): T. Row (T,F): F. Row (F,T): T. Row (F,F): F.
Final column: T, F, T, F.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Implication is false only when p ∨ ¬q is T but q is F.

quick_checks.question: How many rows in a truth table with 4 atoms?
Which is FALSE?
quick_checks.explanation: Implication is false only when hypothesis is T and conclusion is F.

quick_checks.question: The contrapositive of p → q is:
quick_checks.explanation: Flip and negate both parts; the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.

key_takeaways: A truth table with n atoms has 2ⁿ rows; build column by column.
p → q is false ONLY when p is T and q is F.
Many English phrases ('only if', 'whenever', 'sufficient', 'necessary') all translate to →.
p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p (contrapositive); but p → q ≢ q → p (converse).
p ↔ q is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value.
summary.next: You now have the full Module 1 toolkit. Move to the **Module 1 Exercises** for lab- and exam-style drills.

exercises.title: Module 1 Exercises — Propositional Logic
exercises.description: Practice problems modeled on CPCS 222 Labs 01–03, Assignment 1, and the Spring 2026 midterm. Includes proposition classification, truth-table construction, English-to-logic translation, converse/inverse/contrapositive transformations, tautology proofs by rules, exam-style passages, and randomized drills.

questions.question: Which of the following IS a proposition?
questions.explanation: Declarative + definite truth value (T).
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q1 — proposition classification.

questions.question: If p is false and q is true, what is p ∨ q?
questions.explanation: Inclusive ∨ is true when at least one operand is true.

questions.question: If p is T and q is F, what is p → q?
questions.explanation: Implication is false ONLY in this configuration.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 02 / midterm truth-table patterns.

questions.question: The contrapositive of 'If you study, then you pass' is:
choices: If you pass, then you study.
If you do not pass, then you did not study.
If you do not study, then you do not pass.
questions.answer: If you do not pass, then you did not study.
questions.explanation: Contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q3 — CCI in English.

questions.question: How many rows in a truth table with 5 atomic variables?
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q5 — count rows for compound propositions.

questions.question: Which English phrase does NOT translate to p → q?
questions.explanation: 'q is sufficient for p' means q → p, not p → q.

questions.question: p ↔ q is FALSE when:
choices: Both p and q are T.
Both p and q are F.
p and q have different truth values.
Either p or q is T.
questions.answer: p and q have different truth values.
questions.explanation: Biconditional rewards 'sameness' of truth values.

questions.question: Which connective is **inclusive** 'or'?
questions.explanation: ∨ is inclusive — true when at least one is true. ⊕ is exclusive.

questions.question: (p ⊕ q) ∧ (¬r ∨ p) when p = T, q = T, r = T:
questions.explanation: p ⊕ q = F (both T), so the whole ∧ is F.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q2 truth-table values.

questions.question: From the passage 'Open the gate. KAU is in Jeddah. x + 1 = 5.', how many sentences are propositions?
questions.explanation: Only 'KAU is in Jeddah' is a proposition; the others are a command and an open sentence.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q1 — passage-style 'pick the propositions'.

questions.question: Every false sentence is a proposition.
questions.explanation: Only declarative sentences with definite truth values qualify.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q1 — distinguishing proposition vs not.

questions.question: p → q is logically equivalent to ¬q → ¬p.
questions.explanation: Contrapositive equivalence.

questions.question: p → q is logically equivalent to q → p.
questions.explanation: The converse is NOT equivalent to the original.

questions.question: If p is F, then p → q is T regardless of q.
questions.explanation: Vacuous truth.

questions.question: p ⊕ q is T when both p and q are T.
questions.explanation: Exclusive or is T when EXACTLY one is T.

questions.question: The English word 'but' translates to ∧ in logic.
questions.explanation: Stylistic difference only.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q3 — 'below freezing but not snowing'.

questions.question: ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q.
questions.explanation: Negation of an implication is the broken-promise row.

questions.question: (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q) is logically equivalent to p ⊕ q.
questions.explanation: Standard expansion of exclusive or.

questions.question: Why is 'x > 5' not a proposition?
questions.answer: Because x is a free variable; without a specific value the sentence has no definite truth value.
questions.explanation: Open sentences become propositions only after their variables are bound or assigned.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q1 — open-sentence trap.

questions.question: Translate to logic: 'You can enter the exam only if you have your student ID.' (e = enter, s = have ID.)
questions.explanation: 'p only if q' means p → q; the ID is necessary for entry.

questions.question: State converse, contrapositive, and inverse of 'If it is sunny, then we go to the park.'
questions.answer: Converse: 'If we go to the park, then it is sunny.' Contrapositive: 'If we do not go to the park, then it is not sunny.' Inverse: 'If it is not sunny, then we do not go to the park.'
questions.explanation: Original p → q. Converse q → p; contrapositive ¬q → ¬p; inverse ¬p → ¬q.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q3 / Assignment 1 Q3.

questions.question: Use De Morgan to negate: 'It is below freezing AND it is snowing.'
questions.answer: 'It is not below freezing OR it is not snowing.'
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 02 Q8 — De Morgan negation.

questions.question: Why do we have separate symbols ∨ and ⊕ when English uses just one word, 'or'?
questions.answer: Because English 'or' is ambiguous between inclusive ('or both') and exclusive ('but not both'). Logic uses ∨ for inclusive and ⊕ for exclusive so that every formula has exactly one meaning.
questions.explanation: Ambiguity in natural language is resolved by using two distinct symbols.

questions.question: Translate: 'If the bus AND Uber are parked at the bus station, then passengers can travel to Riyadh.' (b, u, t.)
questions.explanation: Conjunction inside the hypothesis; implication to the conclusion.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Assignment 1 Q2.

questions.question: Construct a complete truth table for (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬p, with columns for each subexpression.
questions.answer:
p | q | p∨q | ¬p | (p∨q)∧¬p
T | T |  T  | F  |    F
T | F |  T  | F  |    F
F | T |  T  | T  |    T
F | F |  F  | T  |    F
The compound is true only on (F, T).
questions.explanation: Build column by column.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q6 — truth-table construction.

questions.question: Construct a truth table for (a ⊕ ¬b) ↔ (¬a → c) with three variables.
questions.answer:
a | b | c | ¬a | ¬b | a⊕¬b | ¬a→c | (a⊕¬b)↔(¬a→c)
T | T | T |  F |  F |   T  |   T  |    T
T | T | F |  F |  F |   T  |   T  |    T
T | F | T |  F |  T |   F  |   T  |    F
T | F | F |  F |  T |   F  |   T  |    F
F | T | T |  T |  F |   F  |   T  |    F
F | T | F |  T |  F |   F  |   F  |    T
F | F | T |  T |  T |   T  |   T  |    T
F | F | F |  T |  T |   T  |   F  |    F
Final column: T, T, F, F, F, T, T, F.
questions.explanation: Eight rows for three variables.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Assignment 1 Q1.

questions.question: Show that (p → q) ∨ (p → ¬q) is a tautology using a truth table.
questions.answer:
p | q | ¬q | p→q | p→¬q | (p→q)∨(p→¬q)
T | T |  F |  T  |   F  |     T
T | F |  T |  F  |   T  |     T
F | T |  F |  T  |   T  |     T
F | F |  T |  T  |   T  |     T
Every row is T → tautology.
questions.explanation: When p is F both implications are vacuously T; when p is T exactly one of q, ¬q is T.

questions.question: Use rules of equivalence to show that ¬p → (q → r) ≡ q → (p ∨ r).
questions.explanation: Use p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q twice; rearrange.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 03 Q5.

questions.question: Determine whether ¬(p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)) and (¬p ∧ ¬q) are equivalent using rules.
questions.explanation: De Morgan, distributive, identity.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 03 Q7.

questions.question: Are these specifications consistent? S1: 'The diagnostic message is stored OR retransmitted.' S2: 'The message is NOT stored.' S3: 'If stored, then retransmitted.'
questions.answer: Let p = stored, q = retransmitted. Specs: p ∨ q, ¬p, p → q. Try p = F, q = T: p ∨ q = T, ¬p = T, p → q = T (vacuously). All true → CONSISTENT.
questions.explanation: Find one assignment satisfying every spec.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 02 Q9 — consistency check.

questions.question: Read the passage and identify the **non-propositions**: 'Sara arrived at KAU before her CPCS 222 lecture. The library opens at 7:30 AM. Please silence your phone. 12 is divisible by 4. She wrote x + 5 = 11 in her notebook. Wow, the lecture hall is full today!'
questions.answer: Non-propositions: 'Please silence your phone' (command), 'x + 5 = 11' (open sentence), 'Wow, the lecture hall is full today!' (exclamation).
questions.explanation: Each fails one of the two property checks.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q1 — KAU/Ahmed passage.

questions.question: For 'Having a valid student ID is necessary for entering the exam', state inverse, converse, contrapositive in English. (s = valid ID, e = enter the exam.)
questions.answer: Original: e → s. Converse (s → e): 'If you have a valid student ID, you can enter the exam.' Contrapositive (¬s → ¬e): 'If you do not have a valid student ID, you cannot enter the exam.' Inverse (¬e → ¬s): 'If you cannot enter the exam, you do not have a valid student ID.'
questions.explanation: 'Necessary' marks the conclusion.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q3.

questions.question: Translate: 'Access is granted only if the user is authenticated AND the data is encrypted.' (s = access granted, q = authenticated, r = encrypted.)
questions.explanation: 'p only if q' means p → q.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q4.

questions.question: Translate: 'The system is secure if and only if either the data is encrypted or the user is authenticated, but not both.' (p, q, r as above.)
questions.explanation: 'Iff' = ↔; 'either…or…but not both' = ⊕.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q4 second sub-question.

questions.question: Show that [p ∧ (p → q)] → q is a tautology using rules of equivalence (not a truth table).
questions.explanation: Eliminate →, simplify.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Assignment 1 Q4.

questions.template: Compute the truth value of {EXPR} given p = {P} and q = {Q}.
questions.instructions: Pick one EXPR, one P, one Q at random; compute.
questions.example_realization: EXPR = p → q, P = T, Q = F → answer F.
questions.explanation: Random drill on small truth-table evaluations.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q6.

questions.instructions: Build 4 rows for two atoms; add intermediate columns.
questions.example_realization: EXPR = (p → q) ∧ (q → p) → final column equals p ↔ q.
questions.explanation: Random truth-table drill.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q6 / Lab 02 Q5–Q7.

P_TEXT: you have a valid student ID

questions.example_realization: RELATION=contrapositive, P_TEXT='you have a valid student ID', Q_TEXT='you can enter the exam' → 'If you cannot enter the exam, then you do not have a valid student ID.'
questions.explanation: Drill on which transformation preserves equivalence (only contrapositive).
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q3.

SENTENCE: p if and only if q

questions.explanation: Random drill on translation phrases.

questions.template: Identify the non-propositions in this passage: '{PASSAGE}'

PASSAGE: KAU is in Jeddah. Close the door. 7 + 5 = 12. What time is the lecture? x = 3. Wow, hot day!
Saudi Arabia borders Jordan. Pay your STC bill. y > 0. 14 is even. Is the gate open?
Riyadh is north of Jeddah. Please answer this. p + q = 5. Hello! 5 is prime.

questions.instructions: Mark commands, questions, exclamations, and free-variable equations as non-propositions.
questions.example_realization: Passage 1 → 'Close the door' (command), 'What time is the lecture?' (question), 'x = 3' (open), 'Wow, hot day!' (exclamation).
questions.explanation: Drill on the passage-style midterm pattern.
